about: Which polity holds each moku in each era. Keys are `island:moku` exactly as boundaries/moku.geojson gives them in mokuKey (island pack id, moku name with the SHPD-corrected spelling of the State GIS ahupuaʻa layer). Kahoʻolawe and Molokini lie inside maui:Honuaʻula. Where a holding is uncertain or contested, `notes` says so; an era-wide note is under the key "_".

polities.name: Hilo and Hāmākua (the chiefs of Hilo, of the line of ʻI)
Maui (from 1783 also Oʻahu and Molokaʻi, under Kahekili)
Ke Aupuni Hawaiʻi, the Hawaiian Kingdom
the Provisional Government (1893) and the Republic of Hawaiʻi (1894–1898)
the United States: Territory (1898), State of Hawaiʻi (1959)

voyaging._: No district holdings are recorded for these centuries; the genealogies name chiefs, not the lands they held.

mailikukahi._: Reign-indexed and soft. Each island is shown as its own chiefdom.
mailikukahi.hawaii:Hilo: Before ʻUmi the districts of Hawaiʻi had their own chiefs under a paramount at Waipiʻo; ʻUmi had to win them by war (Kamakau, ch. I). Shown as one chiefdom; hatch.
mailikukahi.maui:Hāna: Fornander (p. 87) says the Hāna chiefs acknowledged the Maui ruler in Piʻilani's reign "and perhaps during that of his father", implying they stood apart before. Which districts went with Hāna is not recorded; Hāna and Kīpahulu shown.
mailikukahi.lanai:Lāhainā: Lānaʻi stood to Maui as Niʻihau to Kauaʻi: independent at times, acknowledging Maui at others (Fornander, p. 95).
mailikukahi.niihau:Kona: Niʻihau independent at times, acknowledging Kauaʻi at others (Fornander, p. 95).

umi._: Reign-indexed and soft. Hawaiʻi united under ʻUmi; Maui under Piʻilani and Kiha-a-Piʻilani, Hāna included.

kakuhihewa._: Reign-indexed and soft. Kamakau’s map for these generations: the rulers of Kona over Kohala, Kona and Kaʻū only, with other chiefs over Hilo and Hāmākua (pp. 61, 64); Maui under Kamalālāwalu and his heirs; Oʻahu under Kākuhihewa’s line and Kūaliʻi; Kauaʻi under the Kawelo chiefs.
kakuhihewa.hawaii:Hilo: The chiefs of Hilo of the line of ʻI, at war with the rulers of Kona through the reigns of Keakamahana and Keakealani and more often the victors (Kamakau, pp. 61–63; Fornander, p. 128). Lonoikamakahiki held the whole island at the start of the span; Fornander has Keawe win Hilo back by marriage at its end (p. 129), Kamakau has Keawe still ruling only Kohala, Kona and Kaʻū (p. 64). Contested; hatch.
kakuhihewa.hawaii:Hāmākua: With Hilo: Kamakau names the descendants of ʻUmi’s sons as the rulers of Hilo and Hāmākua (p. 61). Contested; hatch.
kakuhihewa.hawaii:Puna: Kamakau names Laʻa, read here as ʻŌlaʻa in Puna, among the lands the Kona chiefs wanted from the Hilo chiefs (p. 62); who held the rest of Puna is not recorded. Hatch.
kakuhihewa.hawaii:Kohala: The Mahi chiefs of Kohala led the war for the rulers of Kona (Kamakau, p. 63; Fornander, pp. 127–129).
kakuhihewa.maui:Hāna: Kamalālāwalu kept his court at Hāna when Lonoikamakahiki visited him (Fornander, p. 122).
kakuhihewa.lanai:Lāhainā: Fornander infers from the legends that Lānaʻi became subject or tributary to Maui under Kamalālāwalu (p. 207); Kūaliʻi of Oʻahu is said to have raided it (p. 282).
kakuhihewa.molokai:Kona: Its own chiefs. Kūaliʻi fought for the Kona chiefs against those of Koʻolau at Kalaupapa and settled their quarrel without taking the island (Fornander, p. 282); by Kaulahea’s reign on Maui its chiefs looked to Maui and Oʻahu for support (p. 210).
kakuhihewa.molokai:Koʻolau: Its own chiefs, beaten at Kalaupapa by Kūaliʻi and the Kona chiefs (Fornander, p. 282).
kakuhihewa.oahu:ʻEwa: Kākuhihewa made the island one; his sons shared it in peace; by Kūaliʻi’s accession the ʻEwa and Waialua chiefs ruled with little regard for the mōʻī until he beat them (Fornander, pp. 273–275, 278–281).
kakuhihewa.oahu:Waialua: As ʻEwa: held apart from the mōʻī before Kākuhihewa and again before Kūaliʻi (Fornander, pp. 272–273, 278).
kakuhihewa.oahu:Waiʻanae: Held by Kākuhihewa’s cousin until the peace and marriage that made the island one (Fornander, p. 273); its chiefs rose against Kūaliʻi and were crushed (p. 281).
kakuhihewa.oahu:Koʻolauloa: Held by Kākuhihewa’s cousin until the peace and marriage that made the island one (Fornander, p. 273).
kakuhihewa.oahu:Koʻolaupoko: The mōʻī’s own lands from Kanekapu’s time: Kūaliʻi was born, lived and died at Kailua (Fornander, pp. 278, 283).
kakuhihewa.kauai:Kona: The Kawelo chiefs: Kawelomahamahaiʻa, Kawelomakualua at Wailua, then the war in which Kawelo-a-Maihunaliʻi, helped from Oʻahu, overthrew Kaweloaikanaka (Fornander, pp. 292–294). Late in the span Kūaliʻi of Oʻahu came to the windward side by inheritance and set Peleioholani over Kauaʻi, while Waimea and the Kona side stayed with Lonoikahaupu’s family (pp. 282, 295–296); the legend has the king of Kauaʻi give the island over to him (Fornander Collection, vol. IV, p. 406). Contested; hatch.
kakuhihewa.kauai:Puna: Late in the span held by Kūaliʻi of Oʻahu by inheritance, with the rest of the windward side (Fornander, p. 295). Contested; hatch.
kakuhihewa.kauai:Koʻolau: Late in the span held by Kūaliʻi of Oʻahu by inheritance, with the rest of the windward side (Fornander, p. 295). Contested; hatch.
kakuhihewa.kauai:Haleleʻa: Late in the span held by Kūaliʻi of Oʻahu by inheritance, with the rest of the windward side (Fornander, p. 295). Contested; hatch.
kakuhihewa.niihau:Kona: With Kauaʻi; at times independent (Fornander, p. 95).

alapai._: Fornander's dates for the 1730s wars are estimates.
alapai.molokai:Koʻolau: Fornander (p. 289) says Peleioholani of Oʻahu brought the Koʻolau chiefs of Molokaʻi to acknowledge him about 1738, "neither very thorough nor very lasting". Contested; hatch.
alapai.molokai:Kona: Alapaʻinui fought the Oʻahu chiefs at Kawela but reinstated the Molokaʻi chiefs rather than annex the island (Fornander, p. 138). Contested; hatch.

kalaniopuu._: Kamakau (p. 92) gives the map at Cook's arrival in 1778: Kaʻeo over Kauaʻi, Kahahana over Oʻahu and Molokaʻi, Kahekili over Maui, Lānaʻi and Kahoʻolawe.
kalaniopuu.maui:Hāna: Held by Hawaiʻi from about 1759 until Kahekili retook Kaʻuiki early in 1782 (Fornander, pp. 146, 215–217).
kalaniopuu.maui:Koʻolau: Fornander (p. 213) says Maui curtailed Hawaiʻi's holdings outside Kaʻuiki, "more especially on the Koolau side". Shown with Maui; contested.
kalaniopuu.maui:Kaupō: Raided by Hawaiʻi in the 1770s; shown with Maui.
kalaniopuu.molokai:Kona: Held by the Oʻahu rulers from 1764–65 until 1783 (Fornander, p. 290).
kalaniopuu.molokai:Koʻolau: Held by the Oʻahu rulers from 1764–65 until 1783 (Fornander, p. 290).

kahekili._: After Mokuʻōhai (July 1782) and Kahekili's conquest of Oʻahu (January 1783). Kamehameha held Maui briefly after Kepaniwai in 1790.
kahekili.hawaii:Hāmākua: Split: Fornander (p. 311) gives "portions of Hamakua" to Kamehameha and the rest to Keawemauhili. Shown with Kamehameha; hatch.
kahekili.hawaii:Puna: Split: part of Puna with Keawemauhili, lower Puna with Keōua (Fornander, p. 311). Shown with Keōua; hatch.
kahekili.hawaii:Hilo: Keawemauhili held Hilo until he was killed about 1790; Keōua then held the east of the island until his death in 1791.
kahekili.kauai:Kona: Kauaʻi under Kaʻeo, Kahekili's brother and ally, not under Kahekili.

kamehameha._: From Nuʻuanu (1795). The kingdom's name and institutions grow through this era.
kamehameha.kauai:Kona: Independent under Kaumualiʻi until the 1810 agreement, then ruled by him under Kamehameha (Kamakau, pp. 194–197).

kauikeaouli._: From 25 February to 31 July 1843 the kingdom was under a provisional British cession (Jarves).

liliuokalani._: The Queen reigned until 17 January 1893. The Provisional Government held power from then, and the Republic of Hawaiʻi from 4 July 1894 (P.L. 103-150).

coda._: Annexed by joint resolution in 1898; a State since 1959. P.L. 103-150 acknowledges that the 1893 overthrow was illegal, and the legitimacy of annexation remains contested. Kahoʻolawe is held by the State in trust for a future Native Hawaiian sovereign entity (UH News 2026; KIRC).
